tagline.text: Boracay's Station 2 seafood market and paluto alley

location.label: Location
location.text: Balabag, Boracay Island (Station 2), between White Beach and the Main Road

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (the market runs year-round)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Kalibo International Airport (KLO) or Caticlan Airport (MPH)

children.text: D'Talipapa is a seafood market tucked behind Station 2 on Boracay. You buy fish, prawns and crab by weight and have a nearby restaurant cook them, a system called paluto, so with a little bargaining know-how you can eat fresh seafood at a fair price.

D'Talipapa is a traditional market you can walk into from Station 2 in the middle of Boracay. In Tagalog, a talipapa is a small neighborhood market, and on Boracay the name has come to mean the seafood market together with the restaurants around it. It sits between White Beach and the island's Main Road, about
south of D'Mall, roughly a
10 minutes
walk. It is one block back from the beach and easy to walk past, but once you step in, fish stalls and restaurants line both sides of a narrow alley.

The heart of the experience is paluto. The word is Filipino for "please cook it for me": you pick the seafood you want at the market, have it weighed and buy it, then take it to a nearby restaurant and ask for it to be cooked the way you like. You pay the vendor for the seafood and the restaurant separately for cooking. It is more hassle than ordering from a menu, but you see the freshness with your own eyes and decide the quantity yourself, which is why it is regarded as one of Boracay's signature food experiences, including among Korean travelers.

The stalls display prawns, crab, lobster, squid, shellfish, and fish such as tuna and snapper on ice. Prices are not fixed; they vary with the day's catch, the weather and the number of customers, and bargaining is the norm. Local guides generally put prawns at about
per kilo and lobster at about

, but these figures swing widely by season and vendors may ask several times as much in peak periods, so treat them only as a rough guide. Opening hours differ from shop to shop, but most places open late morning and stay open until about 9 PM; for the best pick, go in the early morning or late afternoon.

It is not a glamorous attraction. The floor is wet, it smells of fish and the touting is loud. In return, it is the closest thing to local life on the island, and the range of what a meal can cost is wide enough to fit your group's budget. It is also worth a visit to calibrate prices before you order an expensive seafood set at a beachfront restaurant.

blocks.title: Browsing and choosing at the market

children.text: Just strolling the alley and comparing prawns, crab, squid, shellfish and fish laid out on ice is fun in itself. Fresh seafood has clear eyes, bright red gills, firm flesh and a clean sea smell. It is safer to walk past several stalls first and buy afterward.

Carry your seafood to a restaurant around the market and choose a cooking style, such as grilled, steamed, garlic butter, mango sauce or sweet and sour. The same prawns taste different depending on the preparation, so many people order two or three styles. Cooking fees differ by restaurant, so confirm the total before you order.

Knocking down the first price is perfectly natural here. You have the advantage if you buy several kilos at once or several kinds at the same stall. Local guides suggest opening at half to 70% of the vendor's first price, ideally firm but with a smile.

Medium-sized prawns are what travelers recommend most often. They are not expensive and rarely disappoint, whether grilled or in a sauce. Many people eat squid grilled or as adobo, and among fish, steamed lapu-lapu (grouper) is popular.
If you do not have time for a sit-down meal, you can buy charcoal-grilled seafood skewers in the alley. They are a good thing to try a skewer or two of during an evening stroll.

D'Talipapa lies on the route between D'Mall and the Station 2 beach, so shopping, a beach walk and a meal fit together easily. There are also souvenir and beach-gear shops inside and around the market, which suits anyone who enjoys bargaining.

Next to the market you will find large open-air restaurants and smaller, quieter ones. Cooking fees are broadly similar; the differences are atmosphere, cleanliness, cooking skill and speed of service. Groups and families will like places with plenty of space, while couples and small parties may prefer a smaller, calmer spot.

items.title: Lunch paluto route
items.subtitle: A relaxed lunch with fresh ingredients

children.text: Walk to the market from the Station 2 beach or your hotel. The Main Road entrance has a big sign, while the beachside entrance has none, so ask hotel staff for directions.
Do not buy right away; walk the stalls once and compare the price and condition of prawns, crab and fish. This is your chance to get a feel for going rates. Have cash and small bills ready.
Bargain at the stall you like, have the seafood weighed and settle the price. Ask the vendor to hold the scale up so you can see the reading, and you can relax.
Go to a nearby restaurant and agree on the cooking style, the cooking fee and the price of rice and vegetable sides before handing over the seafood.
When it is cooked, the plates arrive. Garlic rice and stir-fried water spinach round it out into a meal.
After the meal, relax on the Station 2 beach or look around D'Mall.

Around noon, vendors may be having their own lunch and it can be quiet, but many people say the early morning is better for choosing fresh stock. For a large group, you can also secure a restaurant table first and then go to the market.

items.title: Sunset dinner route
items.subtitle: Shop in the late afternoon, then have dinner

children.text: After playing at the beach and showering, stop by the market. Some travelers report that late in the afternoon some stalls lower prices a little to clear the day's remaining stock.
Buy mainly prawns, squid and shellfish, and bring them to a restaurant for paluto.
Have an early dinner, then head out to White Beach in time for sunset.
Enjoy dessert or coffee along D'Mall, then head back to your hotel.
Most shops close around 9 PM. Late in the evening, the variety of seafood may be smaller.
Direct flights run from Manila (NAIA) to Caticlan Airport (MPH, officially Godofredo P. Ramos Airport) in about
1 hour
. The Caticlan jetty is close to the airport.
Flying into Kalibo International Airport (KLO) is often cheaper, but you then need a further
1.5–2 hours
by van or bus to the Caticlan jetty.
Flights and fares change with the season. Check the airline's latest notices when booking.

items.title: By boat from Caticlan to Boracay

children.text: The boat from the Caticlan jetty to the Cagban terminal on Boracay takes about
15–20 minutes
Terminal fees, the environmental fee and registration procedures change often, so check the latest notices before you travel.
Boat service can be suspended in bad weather. If you have a departure flight, leave at least a day to spare.

items.title: From the island to the market

children.text: Take a tricycle or electric tricycle along the island's Main Road to near Station 2. Always agree on the fare before you board, and check current fares locally.
The market entrance on the Main Road has a sign. The beachside entrance can be reached on foot from the Station 2 beach.
If you are staying at Station 2, you can walk there. From D'Mall it is about
to the south.

The market is open all year, so you can buy seafood whenever you visit. However, high waves or a typhoon keep fishing boats in, which cuts supply and raises prices. Boracay's dry season generally runs from November to May, when the sea is calm and the seafood supply is relatively steady.
During the day, early morning (about
) offers the widest selection, and some travelers say late afternoon (about

) is better for bargaining. Midday is tiring because of the heat and crowds, so it is best avoided. Weekends and holidays are crowded, so weekdays are much calmer. One guide says prawns are in season from October to February and marlin from March to June, but this comes from a single source, so treat it as a rough guide.

You eat at the restaurants right next to the market. Local guides describe Plato D' Boracay, a large open-air restaurant by the market, as good for groups and families, and Blue Jade Cafe behind it as quiet. Sowerby's, the Talipapa branch of Guilly's Island, and Boracay I-Land Seafood Restaurant are also often recommended. Restaurant ratings change often, so check recent reviews.

In general, even the same cooking style differs in price and taste from one restaurant to another, so before buying seafood, decide which restaurant will cook it and ask about the cooking fee first. Garlic rice and stir-fried water spinach can be added at most restaurants. Hotels and resorts at Station 2 are close by, and D'Mall is within walking distance, so it is easy to walk back after a meal.
Bring plenty of cash. Most stalls do not take cards, and there are ATMs nearby. Change can be short, so carry small bills.
Do not pay the first price. Local guidance suggests countering at half to 70% of the vendor's opening price. Compare the prices at two or three stalls before deciding.
Check the scale with your own eyes, and ask the vendor to hold it up so you can read the display.
Before buying seafood, agree which restaurant will cook it and what the total cooking fee will be. Even at the same restaurant the price depends on the weight and kind of seafood.
Judge freshness by clear eyes, bright red gills, firm flesh and a smell that is not too fishy.
The floor is wet, so wear sandals or sneakers with non-slip soles. Avoid loose slippers whose straps come undone.
Do not touch the fish on display before the vendor invites you to. It is polite to ask before taking photos, too.
If you want to take leftover seafood with you, bring a cooler or insulated bag. If your room has no fridge, buy only what you will eat.
One person usually eats less than you expect. Start with 500 g to 1 kg and add more if you need it.
Reviews often mention being asked for a much larger amount afterward when the price and cooking fee were not settled before the seafood was handed over. Always confirm the total first.
Some reviews say the opening price can be set higher for foreigners. Comparing and bargaining matter.
Restaurants charge the cooking fee separately by weight or by number of dishes, so remember the total weight of the seafood you bought at the market.
Some shops may have closed or changed names. Do not rely only on the restaurant names in guides; confirm on site.
Seafood spoils easily. If you doubt the freshness of raw seafood, do not buy it. If you have allergies, always check the ingredients.
Do not rush a decision under the pressure of touting and bargaining. Take your time and compare calmly.
Opening hours, rules and going prices change often. Check the latest notices and the situation on site.

A quiet beach on the north of the island, reached by tricycle (travel time depends on traffic). It works well as a half-day outing combined with a visit to the market.

north of the market. Souvenirs, money changers and cafes are clustered here, making it a pleasant stroll after a meal.
